title: White House Meeting: Space & AI Policy
summary: Working meeting on space and AI policy ahead of the November Mars window. Agreed on a presidential statement supporting the uncrewed Mars mission, a 90-day interagency fast-track for grid interconnection on AI data centers, and continued Starlink participation in the Golden Dome architecture study. Musk pushed back on a proposed AI chip export change; the item was tabled for a follow-up with the Commerce Department.
decisions: The White House will issue a statement of support for the November uncrewed Mars mission, framed as an American milestone
Launch a 90-day interagency fast-track pilot for grid interconnection permits on AI data centers over 500 megawatts
Starlink stays in the Golden Dome architecture study; procurement terms handled separately by the Pentagon
AI chip export rule change is tabled pending a technical briefing with Commerce

action_items.task: Circulate the Mars statement draft to NASA and OSTP for sign-off
Send the White House the interconnection delay data for the Memphis and Texas sites
Schedule the Commerce technical briefing on chip export rules with xAI and the other labs

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Elon, good to see you. Sit down. Everybody's talking about Mars. November, right? They tell me November. Is it going to happen? Because I'd love it to happen, it would be a beautiful thing.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: November to early December, that's when the planets literally align — the transfer window. Five uncrewed Starships, each carrying Optimus robots. No astronauts this window; the robots go first, prove we can land, then people follow in 2028 or 2030.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Robots on Mars. American robots on Mars. You know what that does? Nobody else is even close. Not China — China's going to the Moon, they say 2029, we'll see. And we're going to Mars with robots. That's a great story, Elon, that's a tremendous story.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: It is, and to be clear about what I'm asking for — I'm not here for money. The mission is privately funded. What matters is that the government doesn't accidentally slow it down. The FAA licensing has actually been good this year, credit where due. My ask is a statement of support from you before the window, because it steadies everyone downstream — regulators, insurers, even my own suppliers move faster when they know it's a national priority.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Susie, we can do a statement. Something big. Maybe I come to the launch. Can I come to the launch?

transcript.speaker: Susie Wiles
transcript.text: We can draft the statement this week and circulate it through NASA and OSTP so the whole space community is aligned behind it. On attending the launch — let's hold that decision until closer, sir, for scheduling and security. The statement is the part with real policy value and no downside.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Fine, statement first, launch maybe. Now, NASA. Some people at NASA are saying you're taking money from the Moon program for Mars. I hear it, people call me, they say Artemis this, Artemis that. What do I tell them?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Tell them the Mars mission doesn't use a dollar of NASA money — it's separate ships, separate funding. And the refueling flights we run for Mars this fall are the exact technology NASA needs for the Artemis lunar landing anyway. Every Mars tanker flight retires risk on their mission for free. Gwynne Shotwell is briefing the administrator's office directly so NASA hears it from us, not from the press.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Good, because I want both. Moon and Mars. I don't want to hear it's one or the other — weak thinking. We do both, we do them bigger than anyone. Okay, next thing. AI. Everybody's building these data centers, gigantic things, and everyone who comes in here says the same word to me. Power. They all say power.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Because it's the real constraint. The chips exist, the buildings go up in months, but grid interconnection — just permission to plug into the grid — takes two to four years. At our Memphis site we self-generated with turbines because the interconnect queue was longer than the entire project timeline. The US will not lose the AI race on talent or chips. If we lose it, we lose it on electricity paperwork.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Electricity paperwork. That's the whole problem? Because that I can fix. We're very good at fixing paperwork, we've been cutting it everywhere. Susie, what can we actually do here, what's real?

transcript.speaker: Susie Wiles
transcript.text: There's an existing authority for critical infrastructure fast-tracking. We could stand up a 90-day interagency pilot — DOE, FERC, EPA in one review lane — for AI data centers above a threshold, say five hundred megawatts. It doesn't change environmental standards, it forces the agencies to run their reviews in parallel instead of in sequence. Legal has looked at similar structures before.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Parallel instead of sequential review would genuinely cut a year or more. I'll send your office the actual delay data from our Memphis and Texas builds — real numbers, which queue, how many months at each stage. Use it as the evidence base. And to be clear, this shouldn't be an xAI favor. Every lab building at scale hits the same wall. Make it industry-wide or it'll die in court and it should.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Industry-wide, fine, everybody benefits, but everybody's going to know who got it done. Okay. Golden Dome. The missile shield. The Pentagon people tell me they want Starlink in it, some people tell me they don't want one company doing too much. Where are we?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: We're in the architecture study alongside the traditional contractors. My position is simple: we already fly more satellites than everyone else on Earth combined, and the sensor layer for missile tracking needs exactly the mass-manufactured satellite capability we've built. But I'd actually agree it shouldn't be one company end to end. Let us do what we're provably best at — the constellation layer — and compete the rest.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: That's reasonable. See, people say you want everything, and here you are saying you don't want everything. I'll tell the Pentagon to keep it moving. If the shield works, it's the biggest thing since Reagan, bigger, because his never got built and mine will.

transcript.speaker: Susie Wiles
transcript.text: On process, sir — Starlink's role stays inside the Pentagon's normal procurement so it's clean. What this meeting can decide is only that the study continues with them in it, and that's already the department's position, so nothing new is needed today.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Fine, clean, keep it clean, but keep it fast. Now, one more, and you're not going to like this one, Elon, people told me you don't like it. The chip thing. Commerce wants to loosen some of the export rules on the AI chips, sell more of them overseas, and some of your competitors are pushing for it hard. Big money says do it. What do you say?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I say be careful with the top-end chips specifically. I'm generally the free-trade guy in the room, and export revenue funds American chip R&D, that part of the argument is real. But frontier AI capability tracks compute almost linearly right now. Selling the newest generation abroad in volume is selling the lead itself. Sell the previous generation freely, keep the frontier tier restricted for a couple of years. It's the difference between exporting cars and exporting the factory.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Exporting the factory, that's good, I understand that one completely — I've been saying it about factories for forty years. But Jensen was in here two weeks ago saying the opposite, saying if we don't sell, they just build their own and we lose the customers and the money. Smart guy, also very convincing. One of you is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: We might both be partly right, which is worse, because then it's a real tradeoff. That's why this shouldn't get decided in a room based on who visited last. Get Commerce to run a technical briefing — all the labs, the chip makers, actual capability projections on the table. I'll show up in person and make my case next to Jensen's. If my argument loses on the merits, fine.

transcript.speaker: Susie Wiles
transcript.text: That's the right structure. I'll set the Commerce briefing for the week of the 11th, all the major labs and both chip positions represented. Sir, we hold the rule change until after that briefing — it's two weeks, and it keeps us from getting whipsawed publicly by whoever's in the building that day.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Two weeks, fine, tabled. But it gets decided this month, I don't do the thing where it's studied forever. Okay Elon, what did I forget? You always have one more thing, everybody who comes in here has one more thing.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: One more thing: spectrum. Starlink's direct-to-phone service needs the FCC to finish the pending spectrum-sharing order. It's not controversial, it's just slow, and it matters for rural coverage — genuinely your voters, statistically speaking. A nudge on timing would put satellite phone service over every dead zone in America a year earlier.

transcript.speaker: Donald Trump
transcript.text: Phone service everywhere, farmers love it, I love it. Susie, find out where it's stuck. Okay. So — statement on Mars this week, the power paperwork pilot, Pentagon keeps moving on the Dome, chips in two weeks with you and Jensen in a room like a heavyweight fight, honestly I might attend that one myself. Good meeting. Elon, land the robots. If a robot walks on Mars while I'm President, I'm putting it in every speech for the rest of my life.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: If the robot walks on Mars, Mr. President, you'll have to get in line behind me. Thank you both — I'll have the Memphis power data to Susie's office by Friday.
